item.title: The Witcher 3: Reason of State Quest (Best Choice)
item.description:
Geralt has gotten himself entangled in politics with Vernon Roche, Dijkstra, and other members of the Temerian patriots as they attempt one final assassination of King Radovid. There's one pivotal choice in Reason of State for The Witcher 3 that determines who wins the war , and that depends entirely on who you side with. Below, we'll share all outcomes of this quest and which choice you should make for the best ending!

The Witcher 3: Blindingly Obvious (Best Choices)

If you make the right choices in Blindingly Obvious, you'll unlock a secret side quest that holds immense consequences for the entire war!

By Jake Fillery

How to Start Reason of State in The Witcher 3

To start Reason of State, you will first have to meet these key requirements:

  • Complete "A Deadly Plot", which is made available after completing Triss Merigold's quests (A Matter of Life and Death & Now or Never).
  • Complete "An Eye for an Eye" and "Redania's Most Wanted".
  • During "Blindingly Obvious", make sure to tell Dijkstra: Tell you what the emperor's after if you let us go.

Provided that you have completed these missions, Reason of State will become available in your Secondary Quests tab. So the earliest you can start this quest is in Act 3 during Final Preparations. You must also complete this quest BEFORE "On Thin Ice".

Should You Help Kill Radovid?

Yes, you should definitely help kill Radovid, as there's no negative consequence for Geralt in Nilfgaard, because there are no witnesses to this. Plus, Radovid has lost his mind, and he's begun using witch hunters to kill mages, dwarves, and anything he deems a threat to humans. To make sure you're on the right path, select these dialogue options in the meeting:

  • Let's say Radovid bites. What then?
  • I'm in.

Best Choice in Reason of State (Should You Let Dijkstra Kill the Temerian Patriots?)

No, you should not let Dijkstra kill Roche and the other Temerian patriots . To save Roche and the Temerian patriots, select the dialogue option: " Won't let you kill them. " This will force you to kill Dijkstra, but it saves the same people who put their lives on the line to help protect Ciri in The Battle of Kaer Morhen.

The reason you should side with Roche and not Dijkstra is for a few reasons, but the first and foremost reason is loyalty. Roche has been a valuable ally, and the fact that he risked his life to help you protect Ciri from the Wild Hunt is reason enough, whereas Dijkstra just gave you pointless coin.

Another major reason is that the Temerian alliance has made a deal with Emhyr, where Nilfgaard claims Aerdirn and Lyria, but Temeria gets to remain self-ruled with its own courts, administrative structures, and army. This is a major win for Temeria, and the only safe choice to make against an unstoppable army.

All Choices & Outcomes in Reason of State

If you don't want to side with Roche and the Temerian patriots, then you can see what happens with all outcomes shown below:

Choice

Outcome

Geralt refuses to help kill Radovid

Radovid wins the war against Nilfgaard, which results in further genocide for all non-humans, mages, and wizards.

Geralt lets Dijkstra kill Roche

Dijkstra becomes the ruler of Redania and manages to win the war against Nilfgaard, bringing a new age of peace and order to the North, including restoring Temeria.

Geralt kills Dijkstra to protect Roche

Nilfgaard wins the war, but enters a truce with Temeria that lets it keep its independence as long as it stops the guerrilla warfare.

See all the other ending differences and outcomes here: The Witcher 3: All Endings & How to Get Them (& DLCs)

item.title: LEGO Fan Transforms 3-in-1 Dolphin Set into Millennium Falcon Build Without Extra Pieces
item.description:
A LEGO fan has shared an impressive build in which they created Star Wars ' Millennium Falcon from a 3-in-1 Dolphin set, with no additional pieces. The conversion of the LEGO kit has impressed many fans for its creativity and the ingenuity required for repurposing pieces so efficiently.

There's always something new to look forward to from LEGO, but some arrivals take longer than others. A recent leak appears to have revealed that two exciting LEGO Star Wars sets have been delayed to 2028. If accurate, it's likely to disappoint fans of the franchise, but builders like this one find ways to make their own Star Wars creations utilizing what they already have.

LEGO Fan Shares Jaw-Dropping Cthulhu MOC Build

A LEGO fan shows off an incredible MOC build of Lovecraftian horror Cthulhu, featuring a stunning diorama of the mythical entity.

By Michael Brandon Ingram

A Dolphin Becomes a Millennium Falcon in LEGO Alternate Build

A well-known LEGO builder has shared their reworked version of the 3-in-1 LEGO Dolphin Creator set. Minute_Food_2881 revealed the remarkable alternate build, which completely changes the set into a scene out of Star Wars . The original set is designed to be built as a pair of dolphins, a seahorse, or as a crab, but instead has been repurposed into the Millennium Falcon and a Y-wing. The creative repurposing of the kit's 542 pieces has impressed the community quite a bit. Those who are interested in trying their hand at reworking the kit the same way can also pick up the Lego MOC from Minute_Food_2881.

Those who lack the LEGO Dolphin Creator set but are in the mood to build a Star Wars creation like this aren't alone. Reworking existing LEGO sets into the Millennium Falcon has become a fairly popular trend in the community, and this isn't the first instance of Minute_Food_2881 doing so. However, there have also been plenty that look beyond Solo's ship, with one recent redux converting a LEGO Golden Retriever set into Tatooine, complete with a Landspeeder and Bantha.

Minute_Food_2881 is no exception here, as he's previously reworked the official Millennium Falcon set into the UNSC Burden of Proof ship from Halo: Campaign Evolved . In a separate instance, he took the same kit and built it into an AT-M6 from Star Wars , instead. With enough creativity and patience, it seems the sky is the limit for reimagining existing LEGO kits.

In addition to a new Star Wars Jedi figure landing later in 2026, the series will be making a comeback by way of Kingdom Hearts . A Kingdom Hearts 4 achievement leak on Steam revealed that players will be visiting a galaxy far, far away. While not much is known about the sci-fi series' involvement past that point, it's been exciting for fans of both Star Wars and Kingdom Hearts nonetheless.

item.title: 6 Best NES RPGs With Progression Systems That Still Hold Up Today, Ranked
item.description:
I think it's easy to look back at RPG s from the NES era and assume their progression systems probably amount to little more than fighting enough enemies to gain a level, buying the next strongest weapon in town, and then doing the whole thing over again until the credits roll. To be fair, there are plenty of games from the era where that isn't too far from the truth. However, there are also some NES RPGs that were already doing things with character progression that games are still doing today, whether that meant letting players decide where their next upgrade went or giving them an entirely different way to develop a character after they'd already spent hours building them up.

Of course, I'm not saying every part of these games has aged particularly well, because anyone who has gone back to an NES RPG after becoming accustomed to modern conveniences knows exactly how rough some of them can be. I'm specifically talking about their progression systems here, and whether getting stronger still feels satisfying rather than simply necessary. Some of these games give the player considerably more control over that process than others, but all six found a way to make character growth feel like something worth thinking about instead of something that just happens while you're grinding.

These rankings are based specifically on how well each game's progression systems hold up today, rather than the overall quality of the game. This list also sticks to RPGs that received an official NES release in North America.

6 Crystalis

Its Elemental Swords Keep Progression From Being All About Levels

  • Developer: SNK
  • Released: 1990

I actually think Crystalis is a great place to start because, on the surface, its progression is about as familiar as it gets. You defeat enemies, earn experience, gain levels, and gradually become stronger, so anyone who has played an action RPG before is going to understand what it's doing almost immediately. But the part that has aged better for me is how much of the hero's growth is also tied to his four elemental swords, with Wind, Fire, Water, and Thunder eventually becoming much more than four different ways to hit something.

Each sword can be powered up further with its corresponding Ball and Bracelet, giving its charged attacks additional functionality and eventually allowing the player to interact with parts of the world that weren't accessible before. Magic is layered on top of all of that as well, so there is this constant sense that the hero isn't merely becoming better at killing whatever is in front of him. He's gradually gaining more ways to deal with the world around him, and while Crystalis certainly shows its age elsewhere, I don't think that particular style of progression has ever really stopped being satisfying.

5 Dragon Warrior 4

Dragon Warrior 4 Makes Developing a Large Party Feel Worth the Trouble

  • Developer: Chunsoft
  • Released: 1992

I've played plenty of party-based RPGs where I find four characters I like and then immediately forget everyone else exists, and that's part of what makes Dragon Warrior 4 's approach so interesting even now. Rather than dumping a huge cast on the player and expecting them to care about everyone equally, its first four chapters focus on different characters before the entire group comes together around the Hero in Chapter 5. By then, these aren't random party members sitting on a menu somewhere. You've already spent time playing as them, leveling them up, and learning what each one actually brings to the table.

Every Mainline Dragon Quest Game, Ranked

There have been many mainline titles in the Dragon Quest series throughout the years though some stand out above the rest.

2
By Jack Mitchell Walker

And once everyone does finally come together, Dragon Warrior 4 has the Wagon to help keep those characters involved. Party members traveling in it can still receive experience after battles in places where the Wagon is available, which means swapping someone into the active group doesn't always come with the immediate realization that they're ten levels behind everyone else. I'll admit this isn't the flashiest progression system on the list, but I think the way the game introduces and develops its cast is a huge reason it works. It gives you plenty of characters to manage without making half of them feel disposable the moment you settle on your favorites.

4 River City Ransom

River City Ransom Somehow Made Shopping Part of the Build

  • Developer: Technos Japan
  • Released: 1990

I know River City Ransom looks much more like a beat 'em up than an RPG, and obviously, that's a massive part of what it is. However, start digging into how Alex and Ryan actually get stronger and there is a surprisingly involved progression system underneath all the punching, kicking, and weapon throwing. Enemies drop money when they're defeated, which can then be taken into the various shops around River City and spent on food that permanently improves different stats. So, rather than every bit of character growth being handed out automatically through experience points, the player is actually deciding what to buy and where some of that growth is going.

Classic SNES RPG is Making a Comeback After 34 Years

A rare and underrated RPG is officially returning in 2027 with a re-release on PC, PlayStation, and Nintendo Switch 2 nearly 34 years in the making.

By Drew Swanson

Even better, books can be purchased to learn new fighting techniques, which means the money you're earning can eventually change what your character is capable of doing in combat as well. I especially like what this does to the beat 'em up loop, because suddenly fighting another group of enemies isn't only about clearing the screen and moving to the next area. Those enemies are basically funding your next upgrade. Plenty of games have tied progression to an economy since then, but River City Ransom was already making buying a hamburger somehow feel like character building in 1990.

3 Zelda 2: The Adventure of Link

Every Level Asks What Link Actually Needs Next

  • Developer: Nintendo R&D4
  • Released: 1988

Anyone who has spent much time with The Legend of Zelda knows Zelda 2: The Adventure of Link is the odd one out, and its progression system is a pretty big reason why. Unlike the rest of the series, defeating enemies awards Link experience points, and reaching certain thresholds gives the player the opportunity to improve his Attack, Magic, or Life. Attack increases the damage Link deals, Magic reduces the amount of magic his spells consume, and Life reduces how much damage he takes. It's a very small system compared to what most RPGs give us now, but I honestly think its simplicity is part of what has helped it age so well.

The reason is that every upgrade still asks the player a question, even if it's a simple one. If enemies are taking too long to kill, maybe Attack gets the next increase. If Link is getting absolutely demolished every time something touches him, Life suddenly starts looking much more attractive. Magic becomes increasingly valuable as more spells enter the picture too, so the answer isn't always going to be the same throughout the game. Zelda 2 obviously isn't going to give anyone hours of buildcrafting, but I don't really need it to. It gives players three obvious ways to improve Link and then lets them decide which problem they want to solve first.

2 Final Fantasy

Final Fantasy Starts Building the Party Before the Game Even Begins

  • Developer: Square
  • Released: 1990

The original Final Fantasy doesn't even wait until the first battle to start asking the player to make decisions about character progression, because choosing the party is quite literally one of the first things you do. There are four Warriors of Light to fill and six classes to choose from, including the Fighter, Thief, Black Belt, Red Mage, White Mage, and Black Mage. You can obviously build something fairly balanced, but you don't have to, and whatever you decide there is going to follow you for the rest of the game. Even before gaining a single level, you've already decided what kind of party you're going to be developing.

Final Fantasy & 4 Other RPGs Officially Unplayable Nowadays

As Square Enix prepares to shut down two Final Fantasy games, let's look back at a few RPGs that we can no longer officially play.

By Mark Sammut

Magic adds another interesting wrinkle because each magic level has four spells available while a character can only learn three, so even spell progression eventually asks the player to leave something behind. Then there is Bahamut's class promotion later in the game, which upgrades every member of the party into a stronger version of their original class. Fighters become Knights, Thieves become Ninjas, Black Belts become Masters, and the three Mage classes become their respective Wizards, with some of those promotions even opening up additional magic use. For an RPG this old, there is still a surprising amount of ownership over how that party comes together, and I think that's what keeps its progression from feeling nearly as old as the game itself.

1 Dragon Warrior 3

Changing Classes Lets an Old Character Become Something Completely New

  • Developer: Chunsoft
  • Released: 1992

Dragon Warrior 3 could have probably made this list on party creation alone, seeing as how the Hero can recruit companions from several different classes and build a group around whatever approach the player prefers. But the reason I think it belongs at the top is what happens much later, once those characters have already had plenty of time to grow. After reaching Dharma, party members who have reached Level 20 can change classes, which sends them all the way back to Level 1 and effectively asks the player to start developing them again. I know that probably sounds like the opposite of progress, but this is where the whole system gets good.

Changing classes cuts a character's stats down, but it also lets them keep spells they already learned, so the new Level 1 character isn't really starting over at all. Instead, you're taking everything you already put into them and using it as the foundation for something else. A character who spent their first life learning magic can eventually move into a different class while keeping those spells, and suddenly the hours you already invested in them have opened another route rather than reaching a dead end. Plenty of RPGs have gone much deeper with job systems since then, but I still love the basic idea Dragon Warrior 3 was working with here. Sometimes the most satisfying way to keep progressing isn't to keep climbing upward. Sometimes it's going back to Level 1 and seeing what you can build the second time around.

Even better, books can be purchased to learn new fighting techniques, which means the money you're earning can eventually change what your character is capable of doing in combat as well. I especially like what this does to the beat 'em up loop, because suddenly fighting another group of enemies isn't only about clearing the screen and moving to the next area. Those enemies are basically funding your next upgrade. Plenty of games have tied progression to an economy since then, but River City Ransom was already making buying a hamburger somehow feel like character building in 1990.

3 Zelda 2: The Adventure of Link

Every Level Asks What Link Actually Needs Next

  • Developer: Nintendo R&D4
  • Released: 1988

Anyone who has spent much time with The Legend of Zelda knows Zelda 2: The Adventure of Link is the odd one out, and its progression system is a pretty big reason why. Unlike the rest of the series, defeating enemies awards Link experience points, and reaching certain thresholds gives the player the opportunity to improve his Attack, Magic, or Life. Attack increases the damage Link deals, Magic reduces the amount of magic his spells consume, and Life reduces how much damage he takes. It's a very small system compared to what most RPGs give us now, but I honestly think its simplicity is part of what has helped it age so well.

The reason is that every upgrade still asks the player a question, even if it's a simple one. If enemies are taking too long to kill, maybe Attack gets the next increase. If Link is getting absolutely demolished every time something touches him, Life suddenly starts looking much more attractive. Magic becomes increasingly valuable as more spells enter the picture too, so the answer isn't always going to be the same throughout the game. Zelda 2 obviously isn't going to give anyone hours of buildcrafting, but I don't really need it to. It gives players three obvious ways to improve Link and then lets them decide which problem they want to solve first.

2 Final Fantasy

Final Fantasy Starts Building the Party Before the Game Even Begins

  • Developer: Square
  • Released: 1990

The original Final Fantasy doesn't even wait until the first battle to start asking the player to make decisions about character progression, because choosing the party is quite literally one of the first things you do. There are four Warriors of Light to fill and six classes to choose from, including the Fighter, Thief, Black Belt, Red Mage, White Mage, and Black Mage. You can obviously build something fairly balanced, but you don't have to, and whatever you decide there is going to follow you for the rest of the game. Even before gaining a single level, you've already decided what kind of party you're going to be developing.

Final Fantasy & 4 Other RPGs Officially Unplayable Nowadays

As Square Enix prepares to shut down two Final Fantasy games, let's look back at a few RPGs that we can no longer officially play.

By Mark Sammut

Magic adds another interesting wrinkle because each magic level has four spells available while a character can only learn three, so even spell progression eventually asks the player to leave something behind. Then there is Bahamut's class promotion later in the game, which upgrades every member of the party into a stronger version of their original class. Fighters become Knights, Thieves become Ninjas, Black Belts become Masters, and the three Mage classes become their respective Wizards, with some of those promotions even opening up additional magic use. For an RPG this old, there is still a surprising amount of ownership over how that party comes together, and I think that's what keeps its progression from feeling nearly as old as the game itself.

1 Dragon Warrior 3

Changing Classes Lets an Old Character Become Something Completely New

  • Developer: Chunsoft
  • Released: 1992

Dragon Warrior 3 could have probably made this list on party creation alone, seeing as how the Hero can recruit companions from several different classes and build a group around whatever approach the player prefers. But the reason I think it belongs at the top is what happens much later, once those characters have already had plenty of time to grow. After reaching Dharma, party members who have reached Level 20 can change classes, which sends them all the way back to Level 1 and effectively asks the player to start developing them again. I know that probably sounds like the opposite of progress, but this is where the whole system gets good.

Changing classes cuts a character's stats down, but it also lets them keep spells they already learned, so the new Level 1 character isn't really starting over at all. Instead, you're taking everything you already put into them and using it as the foundation for something else. A character who spent their first life learning magic can eventually move into a different class while keeping those spells, and suddenly the hours you already invested in them have opened another route rather than reaching a dead end. Plenty of RPGs have gone much deeper with job systems since then, but I still love the basic idea Dragon Warrior 3 was working with here. Sometimes the most satisfying way to keep progressing isn't to keep climbing upward. Sometimes it's going back to Level 1 and seeing what you can build the second time around.

item.title: The Witcher 3: Where the Cat and Wolf Play Walkthrough (All Choices)
item.description:
Where the Cat and Wolf Play is an optional quest in The Witcher 3 that revolves around a massacre in the village of Honorton. As Geralt investigates the scene, he discovers that another witcher is responsible for the deaths, but the circumstances behind the attack are more complicated than they initially appear. This guide covers the investigation, all major choices, and the rewards you can obtain.

RELATED

Learn to level up fast in The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt by following basic and advanced tips that go unnoticed.

By Jake Fillery

Where the Cat and Wolf Play Walkthrough in The Witcher 3

Investigating the Massacre at Honorton

After picking up the Contract: The Beast of Honorton, you will need to visit Honorton, which is located east of Claywich or west of Boatmaker's Hut.

Once you arrive at the village, you will find several necrophages. Deal with them, and the quest Where the Cat and Wolf Play will begin. Geralt will then need to use his Witcher Senses to investigate what happened here.

There are four search markers on the map. At the barn, you can find several bodies, one of which Geralt will notice is not a peasant. You can also find a pitchfork here, but be prepared to deal with an alghoul that attacks you while investigating.

Once the area is clear, head to the next house on the right. Inside, you will find a body, a stove you can interact with, and the head of a Leshen. In another nearby hut, you can find a dead dog outside.

While searching around the third hut, a cutscene will play in which a little girl runs past Geralt. Pick up the doll from the ground, then use your Witcher Senses to hear noises coming from the forest. Follow the sound to find the girl.

Finding the Witcher Responsible for the Massacre

The girl will initially refuse to tell Geralt anything. You can either use Axii on her or give her the doll to get her to open up. She will explain that someone who looked a lot like Geralt killed everyone in the village, revealing that the culprit was another witcher. She will also give Geralt a medallion. After speaking with her, Geralt will tell her to stay where she is while he investigates further.

Head toward the next marker on the map and use your Witcher Senses to find footprints leading away from the village. Follow the tracks, dealing with any wolves that attack you along the way, until you eventually find the witcher.

At this point, you will have the option to attack him immediately or listen to what he has to say.

If you decide to hear him out, he will explain that he was promised a substantial payment for his work, but the villagers paid him far less than agreed. They then attempted to kill him, prompting him to slaughter everyone in the village except for the little girl. You can also ask him about the girl, and he will explain that she reminded him of his sister.

Should You Kill or Spare Gaetan?

After hearing his explanation, you will have to decide whether to kill Gaetan or let him go. Each choice offers different outcomes and rewards.

Kill the Witcher

If you decide to kill him, Geralt will fight Gaetan. Before the battle, you can provide him with a Swallow potion to heal himself. However, Gaetan will trick Geralt with a bomb that temporarily blinds him, impairing your vision throughout the fight. Once you defeat him, you will receive XP and can loot his body to obtain the Taigr and the Witcher's Silver Sword.

Spare the Witcher

If you decide to spare him, you will receive XP and unlock the Take What You Want quest, which also rewards you with the Taigr weapon. However, do not immediately continue with Take What You Want. You need to return to Millie first, and you should not travel too far from the quest area, as doing so will fail the quest.

Helping Millie Find a New Home in The Witcher 3

Once you have spared or killed the witcher, return to Millie and speak with her. You can then travel with her to Oreton, where you will find her aunt.

Millie's aunt will ask Geralt to take care of the girl instead, explaining that she does not have enough food to feed all the children under her care. You can offer her 40 Crowns if you want, which will earn you a small amount of XP.

The quest will end here, but you can return to Millie a few days later. She will give Geralt a Thank You Card before heading back to her house.

item.title: The Witcher 3: Ghosts of the Past Walkthrough (All Choices)
item.description:
Ghosts of the Past is an optional quest in The Witcher 3 that can have an impact on a later main story quest. It involves an old acquaintance of Geralt's and gives you the chance to help him settle unfinished business. However, you will want to complete this quest before starting the Isle of Mists main quest, as doing so beforehand will cause Ghosts of the Past to fail. This guide covers the quest's location, encounters, and the choices that determine what happens next.

The Witcher 3: All Endings & How to Get Them

Curious about all the good and bad endings in The Witcher 3's base game and across Hearts of Stone and Blood and Wine? Find them here!

By Jake Fillery

Ghosts of the Past Walkthrough in The Witcher 3

Find Letho's Location

To begin, make your way to Lindenvale , where you will find Dolores Reardon crying. Speak with her to learn about her manor and start the Fall of the House of Reardon contract. You can also begin this contract by picking it up from a notice board or discovering the manor while exploring.

If you have received the contract from Dolores, travel to the manor marked on your map and investigate the area. You will be tasked with dealing with the beasts inside, but upon arriving, you will discover that the area is empty.

One of the main houses has several mines set up around its entrance. Carefully disarm them before heading inside. Go through the doors on the right and watch out for more traps on the floor, along with crossbow traps mounted on the walls.

Continue through the house until you find a ladder that Geralt can use to reach the attic. Upstairs, he will encounter Letho, who explains that he has already dealt with the beasts and is now hiding from assassins.

Help Letho Deal With His Pursuers

As you speak with Letho, a group of men will arrive, prompting him to ask whether you will help him deal with them. Although the game presents two dialogue options, both lead to the same outcome, so you will need to help Letho fight the men.

After the fight, Letho explains that he wants to visit Louis to find out whether he betrayed him. Stick close and follow Letho on horseback to the camp where Louis can be found.

During their conversation, Letho repeatedly accuses Louis of being a traitor. The argument eventually escalates into a fight against a group of enemies. Deal with them before continuing the conversation.

Louis will reveal the location of Vester's men, giving Letho the information he needs. As you leave, you can also attack and kill Louis if you wish, but doing so offers no additional rewards or meaningful consequences.

Decide Letho's Fate

Once you have finished at the camp, follow Letho on horseback again until you reach Lindenvale. Upon arriving, Letho will ask Geralt to stay back while he handles the situation himself.

During the confrontation, Letho will appear to go down, and you will receive two dialogue choices when talking to Vester and his men:

  • You're good as dead
  • Don't want trouble

If you choose the second option, the men will mention taking Letho's head. You can then either step in and fight them or tell them to take his medallion instead.

If you intervene and fight, the encounter proceeds similarly to the first dialogue option. However, if you let the men take the medallion, they will eventually leave.

After the men depart, Geralt will notice that something is not quite right. Letho eventually gets back up and explains that he used Zanuguebarian venom to make himself appear dead. Now that everyone believes he is dead, he can stop hiding from his pursuers and is free.

Choosing the first option will cause Geralt to step in and fight Letho's attackers. After defeating the men, Letho will express his frustration over Vester's death.

Should You Send Letho to Kaer Morhen?

Once the confrontation is over, Letho will explain that he needs to leave the area. Geralt can suggest that he travel to Kaer Morhen or find a place to hide.

Suggest Kaer Morhen: If you tell Letho to head to Kaer Morhen, he will agree to go there. This allows him to appear later and help Geralt during the Battle of Kaer Morhen main story quest.

Let Letho go to Zerrikania: If you do not suggest Kaer Morhen, Letho will talk about travelling to Zerrikania instead. He will leave to pursue his own plans, and you will not have him available to help during the Battle of Kaer Morhen.

With the conversation finished and Letho's next destination decided, Ghosts of the Past comes to an end.
